title: Mid-term: grid search problems
overview: The mid-term exam solutions. All four are grid problems: reachability with DFS, the smallest component area, knight moves with BFS on a chessboard, and printing the BFS path through a maze with a parent array. Together they are a good revision of Modules 2-6.

concepts.explain: Return true from DFS as soon as the target is found, and pass it up through every caller.
Start `min_area = INT_MAX`, update after each DFS, and use a flag to print -1 when no component exists.
A knight has 8 moves; put them in the `direction` list and BFS works unchanged.
Filling `dist` with -1 lets `dist[i][j] == -1` mean "not visited", so no separate `vis` is needed.
Store `path[child] = parent cell` during BFS, then walk back from the destination and mark cells.
When several shortest paths exist, the order of `direction` decides which one BFS records.

files.title: Same component?
files.what: Checks with DFS whether cell D can be reached from cell S through `.` cells.
steps: Read the grid and the two cells.
If either cell is `-`, print NO; if they are the same cell, print YES.
`dfs(si, sj, di, dj)` returns true when it steps on D.
A true result from any child is returned immediately.
files.input_note: `N M`, the grid, then `Si Sj`, then `Di Dj` (sample 2 of the statement).
files.output_note: `YES`: from (0,1) you go right along the top, down the right column and left to (3,2).
files.watch_out: On a 1000x1000 open grid the recursion can go 10^6 deep; BFS avoids that risk.

check.a: A blocked start (or end) cell can never be in a walkable component.

files.title: Minimum area of a component
files.what: DFS measures each `.` component; the smallest area is printed, or -1 if there are none.
files.output_note: `3`: the pieces have 4, 4, 7 and 3 cells; the smallest is the three dots on the right of row 3.

check.q: Why is `flag` needed when `min_area` already exists?
check.a: Without components `min_area` stays `INT_MAX`, which must be turned into -1.

files.title: Knight moves
files.what: BFS from the knight's cell with the 8 knight jumps; the level of the queen's cell is the answer.
steps: For each test case read the board size and both cells.
`bfs` fills `dist` with -1 and sets the knight's cell to 0.
Pop a cell; if it is the queen's cell, return its `dist`.
Push each valid unvisited jump with `dist + 1`; return -1 if the queue empties.
files.input_note: `T`, then for each case: `N M`, knight cell, queen cell. Cases: 8x8 corner to corner, a 2x2 board, and a 3x3 board.
files.output_note: `6` (8x8 corner to corner), `-1` (no knight move fits on a 2x2 board), `1` (one jump from (0,0) to (2,1)).

check.q: Why is BFS, not DFS, right for the minimum number of knight moves?
check.a: Every move costs the same, so BFS levels are the fewest moves.

files.title: Maze path marking
files.what: BFS from R to D with a `path` parent grid, then walks back from D and puts `X` on every `.` cell of the route.
steps: Find R and D while reading; `direction` is right, left, up, down as the statement demands.
`bfs` records `path[child] = {par_i, par_j}` for each new cell.
If D was reached, step back from D using `path` until the parent is R.
Each `.` cell on the way becomes `X`; then the maze is printed.
files.input_note: `N M`, then the maze (sample 0 of the statement).
files.output_note: The route is marked with `X`: from R go up into row 2, right along row 2 to column 3, then up through row 1 to D. R and D keep their letters.
files.watch_out: The `if(s_i == -1 || d_i == -1)` check never fires, because the positions start at 0, not -1. Start them at -1 if you want that guard to work.

check.q: Why does the walk-back stop when the parent equals R instead of when the cell equals R?
check.a: So the loop never tries to mark R itself, and it ends one step early.

recap: Reachability: DFS with early return, or BFS.
Min/max over components: reset a counter before each search.
Change the move list for knights or diagonals.
Path printing on grids: parent grid + walk back.

check_yourself.q: How many moves does a knight have, and how many can go off the board from a corner?
check_yourself.a: 8 moves; from a corner only 2 stay on the board, so 6 go off.

check_yourself.q: How would you print the maze path length instead of marking it?
check_yourself.a: Keep a `dist` grid in BFS and print `dist` at D.

body: This is the mid-term, and all four problems are grids. Before reading any of them, sort out the one question that decides your whole solution: **what is the exam actually asking for?** Four answers, four tools:
intro.trace:
asks for                 use
----------------------   --------------------
can I get there at all?  DFS (or BFS)
how big is this piece?   DFS, count as you go
fewest moves             BFS, the level is it
the route itself         BFS + a parent grid

body: The trap is picking DFS for a shortest-path question. DFS finds *a* way through; it will happily wander round three sides of the grid and arrive. BFS spreads out one ring at a time, so the ring a cell falls in **is** its smallest number of moves. If the words "minimum", "fewest" or "shortest" appear, you want BFS.
Here is the worked reminder. A 3 by 4 grid, `-` is a wall, and you start at the top-left corner:

Fill `dist` with -1, set the start to 0, and push it. Pop a cell, and for each of the four neighbours that is inside the grid and still -1, write the parent's distance plus one and push it. The grid of distances comes out like this:

Look at the top-right cell. On the paper it sits three squares from the start, but the walls force the long way round the bottom, and BFS quietly reports 7. No counting by hand would have got that right.

Two small habits carry most of the marks. First, `dist` filled with -1 doubles as the visited array: `dist[i][j] == -1` means "not seen yet", so there is no second `vis` grid to forget to reset. Second, check `valid(i, j)` **before** you touch `grid[i][j]`, or you read outside the grid and the run dies.
The move list is the only thing that changes between problems. Four directions for a maze, eight for a knight:

The search code does not change at all; only the list it loops over does. On a 2 by 2 board no knight jump fits anywhere, so the queue empties and the answer is -1 - always have an answer ready for "never reached".

For the route itself, keep a `path` grid: when BFS first reaches a cell, store which cell it came from. At the end, start at the destination and keep stepping to the stored parent until you are back home; each cell you pass gets marked. And when several shortest routes tie, the order of your `direction` list decides which one comes out, so use the exact order the statement asks for.

Last things to watch: reset every array between test cases, print -1 (not `INT_MAX`) when nothing was found, and remember that a recursive DFS on a 1000 by 1000 open grid can go a million calls deep - BFS has no such risk. The four solutions below show each of these patterns once.
